title: Large Vessel Vasculitis Revisited: Mechanistic Insights and Advances in Diagnosis and Management
journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
one_line_summary: This contemporary review summarizes advances in understanding mechanisms, multimodality imaging algorithms, and biological immune-targeted therapies for giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis.
key_pearls: **Giant cell arteritis (GCA)** affects older adults (**>70 years**, **2–3:1 female ratio**), with thoracic aortic involvement in **40%–65%** conferring a **17-fold** increased risk of thoracic aortic aneurysm.
**Takayasu arteritis (TAK)** typically manifests in young females aged **10–40 years** (**9:1 female ratio**), commonly causing renal artery stenosis (**24%–68%**) and subclavian steal syndrome.
First-line diagnostic imaging recommendations comprise temporal/axillary **ultrasound** for cranial GCA, **18F-FDG PET** for large-vessel GCA, and **MRI/MRA** for TAK.
The diagnostic accuracy of **18F-FDG PET** declines **significantly** after **3 days** of high-dose glucocorticoid administration.
Targeted **68Ga-DOTATATE PET** binds **SST2** on activated macrophages, bypassing high background physiological uptake in the myocardium and brain to detect coronary and intracranial vasculitis.

Glucocorticoids remain acute first-line therapy, but adjuvant **tocilizumab** or **upadacitinib** (**15 mg daily**) in GCA and **methotrexate/TNF-inhibitors** in TAK **significantly** increase remission rates and facilitate steroid sparing.

sections.heading: Pathological Causes and Clinical Presentations of GCA and TAK
sections.content:
- **Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA)** is the most common vasculitis in adults **>70 years**, with a **2–3:1 female-to-male ratio** and highest incidence in Northern Europe (**21.5 per 100,000**).
- GCA involves panarterial granulomatous inflammation starting in the adventitia via vasa vasorum, mediated by **CD4+ T cells**, **NOTCH-1/JAG1** interaction, matrix metalloproteinases, and deficiency in local **PD-L1** checkpoint expression.
- Cranial GCA presents with headache, temporal artery tenderness, jaw claudication, and visual loss due to anterior or posterior ischemic optic neuropathy or central retinal artery occlusion.
- Large vessel GCA affects **40%–65%** of GCA patients, predominantly involving the thoracic aorta with a **17-fold** higher risk of thoracic aortic aneurysms and a **63%** increased risk of myocardial infarction.
- **Takayasu Arteritis (TAK)** typically affects females aged **10–40 years** (**9:1 female ratio**), with peak prevalence in Asia (**4 per 100,000**).
- TAK pathobiology features vascular dendritic cell activation, toll-like receptor upregulation, intimal hyperplasia, fibroblast proliferation, and smooth muscle cell senescence, causing stenoses and aneurysms.
- TAK angiographic subtypes are classified via Lupi-Herrera or Numano criteria (Types I–V); renal artery involvement occurs in **24%–68%** of cases, causing renovascular hypertension.
- Subclavian stenosis in TAK frequently leads to subclavian steal syndrome, limb claudication, vascular bruits, and pulse discrepancies; up to **30%** present acutely with major ischemic events.
section_pearls: Ischemic jaw claudication and transient vision loss are independent risk factors for permanent vision loss in GCA.
GCA patients have a **17-fold** increased risk for thoracic aortic aneurysm compared to age-matched controls.

sections.heading: Less Common Causes of Large Vessel Vasculitis
sections.content:
- **Behçet's disease** causes focal aortic dilatation rather than diffuse aortitis.
- **Relapsing polychondritis** involves the aorta and coronary arteries, carrying risk of aortic dissection and rupture.
- **IgG4-related disease** presents with aortitis/periaortitis, retroperitoneal fibrosis, autoimmune pancreatitis, or pericoronary soft tissue thickening.
- **Cogan syndrome** causes ocular and vestibuloauditory dysfunction with aortitis; **HSP-70** antibodies are present in **92.9%** of typical cases.
- **VEXAS syndrome** (*vacuoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somatic syndrome*) causes adult-onset autoinflammatory disease with systemic and aortic manifestations in males.
- Infectious causes of aortitis such as **syphilis** and **tuberculosis** must be systematically excluded prior to immunosuppression.
section_pearls: Infectious aortitis (syphilis, tuberculosis) must always be excluded before initiating high-dose immunosuppression.

sections.heading: Diagnostic Pathways and Inflammatory Biomarkers
sections.content:
- Diagnostic algorithms combine clinical risk scores (e.g., Southend pre-test probability score), serum biomarkers, imaging, and histological sampling.
- Serum markers (**CRP** and **ESR**) have a combined sensitivity of **97%** for GCA but low specificity; platelet counts **>400,000/μL** confer a **4.2-fold** increased likelihood of positive temporal artery biopsy.
- **Temporal artery biopsy (TAB)** shows transmural granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells in **43%–75%** of cases, but can be omitted when ultrasound is positive in high clinical suspicion cases.
- **EULAR guidelines** advocate noninvasive imaging over tissue biopsy as the initial diagnostic test when appropriate expertise is available.
section_pearls: Combined CRP and ESR sensitivity for GCA reaches **97%**, while thrombocytosis **>400,000/μL** quadruples positive temporal biopsy likelihood.

sections.heading: Multimodality Vascular Imaging Techniques
sections.content:
- **Ultrasound** shows a pooled sensitivity of **88%** and specificity of **96%** for GCA; the hypoechoic **halo sign** reflects arterial wall edema and resolves rapidly post-steroids.
- **Recommended** ultrasound cut-off values for intima-media thickness are **0.4 mm** for temporal arteries and **1.0 mm** for axillary arteries.
- In TAK, carotid ultrasound demonstrates smooth circumferential echogenic wall thickening known as the **macaroni sign** (sensitivity **81%**, specificity **>90%**).
- **High-resolution MRI/MRA** exhibits **81%** sensitivity and **98%** specificity for cranial GCA, and is the preferred first-line imaging modality for arterial wall and angiographic assessment in TAK.
- **18F-FDG PET** is the primary **recommended** technique for extracranial GCA (sensitivity **76%**, specificity **95%**), demonstrating diffuse, circumferential vascular wall metabolic activity.
- Diagnostic sensitivity of **18F-FDG PET** drops after **3 days** of high-dose glucocorticoid therapy.
- Novel **68Ga-DOTATATE PET** targets **SST2** expressed on activated macrophages, demonstrating **62%** higher signal in active versus inactive vasculitis and reducing background cardiac activity to image coronary vasculitis.
section_pearls: The ultrasound **halo sign** indicates acute arterial edema in GCA and diminishes within one week of glucocorticoid initiation.
**68Ga-DOTATATE PET** allows clear visualization of coronary and cerebral vasculitis due to absent physiological background uptake in myocardium and brain.

sections.heading: Extracranial and Specific Organ Involvement
sections.content:
- **Coronary Artery Involvement**: Present in up to **53%** of TAK patients on CT coronary angiography, predominantly at ostial or proximal locations; noninvasive pericoronary adipose tissue density analysis on CT identifies active coronary arteritis.
- Invasive percutaneous coronary intervention should be deferred during active vasculitis due to heightened risks of stent thrombosis, restenosis, and dissection.
- **Myopericardial Involvement**: Left ventricular systolic dysfunction affects up to **18%** of LVV patients; cardiac MRI utilizing **Lake Louise criteria** (T1/T2 mapping and late gadolinium enhancement) confirms nonischemic myocardial inflammation.
- **Pulmonary Artery Involvement**: Identified in **5.7%–25.9%** of TAK patients, leading to secondary pulmonary hypertension in **25%** of affected cases; manifests as arterial wall thickening, stenosis, occlusion, or peripheral lung infarction.
section_pearls: Percutaneous coronary intervention should be deferred during active vasculitis due to excessive risk of stent thrombosis and arterial dissection.

sections.heading: Contemporary Pharmacotherapy and Disease Management
sections.content:
- **Glucocorticoids**: Acute initial therapy for GCA is **IV methylprednisolone** (for visual symptoms) or oral **prednisolone 40–60 mg daily**, tapered over **12–18 months**; TAK initial therapy is oral **prednisolone 60 mg daily**.
- **Tocilizumab**: IL-6 receptor antagonist strongly **recommended** in GCA to achieve sustained remission and facilitate glucocorticoid weaning; also utilized in refractory TAK.
- **Upadacitinib**: Oral JAK-1 inhibitor (**15 mg daily**) demonstrated **superior** 52-week sustained remission (**SELECT-GCA trial**) combined with a **26-week** steroid taper compared to placebo with a **52-week** taper.
- **Conventional DMARDs**: **Methotrexate**, **azathioprine**, and **TNF inhibitors** (e.g., infliximab, adalimumab) represent mainstays for steroid-sparing therapy in TAK.
- **Secukinumab**: Selective IL-17A inhibitor evaluated in phase 2/3 trials for GCA (*TitAIN*, *GCAPTAIN*) and TAK, showing efficacy in open-label comparisons with TNF inhibitors.
section_pearls: The **SELECT-GCA trial** established that **upadacitinib 15 mg daily** with a **26-week** steroid taper was superior to placebo with a **52-week** taper for sustained GCA remission.

strengths_limitations:
- **Strengths**: In-depth synthesis of pathophysiological mechanisms, validated imaging cutoffs, multimodality diagnostic algorithms, and recent phase 3 clinical trial data for targeted biologics.
- **Limitations**: Narrative review design without quantitative meta-analyses for long-term clinical outcomes across different imaging-guided treatment strategies.

drugs_doses.dose: Intravenous pulses daily for 3 days prior to oral steroids
drugs_doses.indication: Acute giant cell arteritis with ischemic visual symptoms or severe organ-threatening Takayasu arteritis
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Hyperglycemia, acute hypertension, infection, fluid retention, psychiatric disturbances

drugs_doses.dose: 40–60 mg/day orally (GCA without visual loss) or 60 mg/day orally (TAK), tapered over 12–18 months
drugs_doses.indication: First-line remission induction in giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Osteoporosis, cushingoid features, diabetes, hypertension, increased infection risk, adrenal suppression

drugs_doses.dose: 162 mg subcutaneously weekly or 8 mg/kg intravenously monthly
drugs_doses.indication: Relapsing or new-onset giant cell arteritis, and refractory Takayasu arteritis
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Transaminitis, neutropenia, serious infections, gastrointestinal perforation, hyperlipidemia

drugs_doses.dose: 15 mg orally once daily with a 26-week glucocorticoid taper
drugs_doses.indication: Relapsing or new-onset giant cell arteritis
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Upper respiratory infections, herpes zoster reactivation, elevated creatine kinase, potential cardiovascular risks

drugs_doses.dose: 15–25 mg orally or subcutaneously once weekly with folic acid supplementation
drugs_doses.indication: Steroid-sparing maintenance therapy in giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Hepatotoxicity, bone marrow suppression, pulmonary toxicity, GI mucosal ulceration, teratogenicity

drugs_doses.dose: 300 mg subcutaneously weekly loading followed by monthly maintenance
drugs_doses.indication: Investigational IL-17A targeted therapy in giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis
drugs_doses.adverse_effects: Mucocutaneous candidiasis, neutropenia, inflammatory bowel disease exacerbation, nasopharyngitis
